Summary.
Brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) is a neurotrophin that plays fundamental roles in neuronal survival and synaptic plasticity. Its upregulation in the brain can effectively prevent and treat central nervous system (CNS) diseases, including depression, Alzheimer’s disease (AD), and Parkinson’s disease (PD). BDNF is synthesized in various peripheral tissues as well as in the brain and can be transported from peripheral circulation into the brain through the blood–brain barrier. Therefore, foods that upregulate BDNF in peripheral tissues may be beneficial in preventing and treating these CNS diseases. Previously, we revealed that treatment with Chinpi (Citrus unshiu peel) and Citrus natsudaidai increased BDNF levels in the human renal adenocarcinoma cell line ACHN. Here, we evaluated the effects of 21 citrus cultivars on BDNF production in ACHN cells by measuring BDNF levels in the cell culture medium. We found that treatment with peels and pulps of 13 citrus varieties increased BDNF levels in ACHN cells. Treatment with Aurantium, Acrumen, and their hybrids citrus varieties showed a potent BDNF-upregulating effect but not with varieties belonging to Limonellus, Citroph

Many citrus cultivars are consumed worldwide and used in phytotherapy for lifestyle diseases (29, 30), inflammation (31), and cancer (28, 32). However, there is insufficient information regarding the relationship between citrus cultivars and BDNF upregulation.

In this study, we analyzed the effects of the peels and pulps of 21 citrus cultivars on BDNF levels in the culture medium of ACHN cells. Furthermore, we examined the effects of some citrus cultivars on BDNF mRNA expression in ACHN cells.

Screening of citrus peel with BDNF-upregulating effect in ACHN cells.
The relative BDNF levels in the culture medium of ACHN cells treated with each citrus peel sample are shown in Fig. 1. BDNF concentrations in the control were 116.0–261.2 pg/mL. Among the 21 citrus cultivars peel, 13 showed significantly increased BDNF levels in the cell culture medium (Fig. 1). Treatment with citrus hybrids (Sweet spring and Murcott) showed a strong BDNF-upregulation effect equivalent to that of Acrumen (Fig. 1). Treatment with Osmocitrus varieties, such as Yuzu and Sudachi, but not Kabosu, resulted in 1.18- and 1.36-fold higher BDNF levels, respectively, than the control (Fig. 1). Limonellus, Citrophorum, and Cephalocitrus varieties did not elevate BDNF levels in this study (Fig. 1). BDNF concentrations in the culture medium increased depending on the number of ACHN cells (24). We, therefore, confirmed that none of the citrus peel methanol extracts that showed BDNF-upregulating activity significantly increased the viability of ACHN cells (Table 2).

Therefore, many citrus species are expected to increase peripheral BDNF levels by more than 1.3-fold in vivo, and these could be useful in the prevention and treatment of depression.

Some studies have revealed that blood BDNF levels decrease in patients with AD as well as in patients with depression (49–52). Moreover, high serum BDNF levels are related to delayed cognitive decline in patients with AD and in healthy individuals (53, 54). Patients with PD have reduced BDNF levels in the brain (13), indicating that increased levels of BDNF in the brain may contribute to the prophylaxis and treatment of PD. BDNF plays an important role in the survival of dopaminergic neurons and is involved in PD pathophysiology (55). Thus, many citrus species analyzed in this study are potential candidates for the prevention and treatment of AD and PD.

Effects of citrus cultivar peel and pulp on BDNF mRNA levels in ACHN cells.
We examined the transcript levels of BDNF mRNA in ACHN cells treated with peels and pulps of Okitsuwase, Ponkan, Clementine mandarin, and Murcott. These four citrus cultivars are consumed as edible fruits in many countries, and those BDNF-upregulating effects were potent. BDNF mRNA expression in ACHN cells treated with 100 g/mL Okitsuwase, Ponkan, Clementine mandarin, and Murcott peel was 1.68-, 1.48-, 1.44-, and 1.69-fold higher, respectively, than that in the control (Fig. 3).

In the pulp treatment group, BDNF expression in ACHN cells treated with 100 g/mL of Okitsuwase, Ponkan, Clementine mandarin, and Murcott pulp was 2.23-, 1.33-, 1.40-, and 1.67-fold higher, respectively, than that in control (Fig. 3).

Among the 21 citrus cultivars, all Aurantium and Acrumen cultivars induced BDNF upregulation. The BDNF-upregulating effect of these citrus sections tended to be higher than that of other sections; for example, BDNF levels of cells treated with Tankan, King, Kunenbo, Okitsuwase, Ponkan, and Clementine mandarin were 1.36- to 1.93-fold higher than those in the control (Fig. 2). ## 5. Conclusion  
In this study, functional components including flavonoids, phenolic acids, carotenoids, and limonoids were fully analyzed in both pulp and peel from 11 citrus varieties, which were local hybrids and traditional varieties in Zhejiang, to explore the distribution pattern and variability between varieties. Secondary metabolites were far more abundant in the peel than in the pulp, and the accumulation varied significantly between species. Most of these components were correlated with each other. PCA and HCA results showed that citrus varieties were grouped according to these metabolites while also taking citrus peel and pulp into consideration. To the best of our knowledge, this study was the first to provide information on the citrus classification based on four secondary metabolites, and it included citrus peel and pulp. The obtained results filled the data gap for secondary metabolites from local citrus, which could provide data references for citrus resource utilization, selection, and breeding of superior varieties and other research varieties in the future perspective.

Previously, we revealed that the human renal adenocarcinoma cell line ACHN produces and secretes BDNF and is useful in screening for molecular players leading to BDNF upregulation (24). We have shown that treatment with foxtail millet, Citrus unshiu peel (crude drug; Chinpi), and Citrus natsudaidai peel and pulp significantly increased BDNF levels in the culture medium of ACHN cells (24–26). In particular, the increased levels of BDNF by the citrus species were potent, suggesting that citrus plants and cultivars can upregulate BDNF production in ACHN cells.
